query: How is a major repair or major alteration recorded and approved under FAA 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix B?
answer:
Direct answer:
Under FAA 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix B, major repairs and major alterations for products not produced under an FAA approval must be recorded on the repair or alteration form specified in §§ 43.5(b) and 43.9(d); however, such recording is not required for products produced under an FAA approval [S1]. Major repairs and major alterations that have all necessary DER or ODA-approved technical data do not require further approval [S6]. The person intending to perform the work is responsible for obtaining the approved technical data [S2]. A major alteration report describes the work performed, the FAA-approved technical data used, and identifies the individual who performed and/or issued the approval for return to service; this is distinct from a major repair record [S7].

Where to look:
- FAA 14 CFR Part 43 Maintenance (regulation text on recording requirements and exceptions): FAA_14_CFR_Part_43_Maintenance.pdf, location 2 [S1]
- FAA AC 43-210A (data approval guidance for major repairs/alterations): FAA_AC_43-210A_Approval_Major_Repairs_Alterations_Data.pdf, location 5 [S2]
- FAA AC 43-210A (DER/ODA data sufficiency exception): FAA_AC_43-210A_Approval_Major_Repairs_Alterations_Data.pdf, location 10 [S6]
- FAA AC 43.13-2C (alteration data context; note it generally pertains to minor alterations but may be used for major): FAA_AC_43.13-2C_Aircraft_Alterations.pdf, location 14 [S4]

Warnings from the source documents on this topic:
- Do not confuse a major alteration report with other records: "You must not confuse this with a major alteration report, which is a description of the work performed, a description of the FAA-approved technical data used to make the major alteration, and the identification of the individual who performed and/or issued the approval for return to service." [S7]

query: What electrical load analysis requirements apply when performing an aircraft alteration under FAA AC 43.13-2C?
answer:
Direct answer:
Under FAA AC 43.13-2C, the total system load (battery recharging plus system loads) must not exceed the pre-established electrical capacity of the generator system [S8]. Additionally, for repairs or alterations that do not change limitations, procedures, performance, or loading information, a supplement may consist of system operating instructions only, implying such cases may not require full load analysis documentation beyond operational instructions [S7].

Where to look:
- FAA AC 43.13-2C Aircraft Alterations, location 152: "Total system load (battery recharging plus system loads) must not exceed the pre-established electrical capacity of the generator system." [S8]
- FAA AC 43.13-2C Aircraft Alterations, location 19: "Repairs or alterations that do not result in a change to limitations, procedures, performance, or loading information may not require a supplement, or the supplemental information may consist of system operating instructions only." [S7]

Warnings from the source documents on this topic:
Note: The excerpt from UK CAA CAP 562 (S6) states that "non-flight operational loads do not compromise the busbar loading, generator ratings and battery duration," but this is a UK authority document and does not apply to FAA AC 43.13-2C requirements [S6].

query: Is chemical corrosion removal permitted on high-strength aircraft steel under FAA AC 43-4B?
answer:
Direct answer:
Under FAA AC 43-4B, chemical paint removal is permitted as a preferred method for larger areas of metallic surfaces [S1]. However, the document explicitly prohibits using chemical paint strippers containing acid on high-strength steel because such strippers cause hydrogen embrittlement [S2]. The excerpts do not specify which chemical agents are safe for use on high-strength steel beyond excluding those containing acid.

Where to look:
- FAA AC 43-4B_Corrosion_Control_for_Aircraft.pdf, location 87: Paint removal guidance and prohibition of acid-containing strippers on high-strength steel [S1][S2].

Warnings from the source documents on this topic:
- "Do not use chemical paint strippers containing acid because the strippers will cause hydrogen embrittlement on high-strength steel and some stainless steels." [S2]

query: How is intergranular and exfoliation corrosion in 2024 and 7075 aluminum alloys repaired under AC 43-4B?
answer:
Direct answer:
- FAA AC 43-4B prohibits using abrasive blasting to remove intergranular corrosion [S4].
- Exfoliation corrosion is described as an advanced form of intergranular corrosion where surface grains lift due to expanding corrosion products at grain boundaries; AC 43-4B identifies this condition but does not provide repair steps in the supplied excerpts [S1].
- The supplied excerpts do not establish specific repair methods (e.g., chemical treatment, mechanical removal limits, replacement criteria) for intergranular or exfoliation corrosion in 2024/7075 under AC 43-4B; the cited passages prohibit abrasive blasting for intergranular corrosion [S4] and describe exfoliation [S1].
- NASA-STD-6016C notes that certain aluminum-magnesium alloys can be susceptible to exfoliation corrosion but does not give repair instructions for aircraft structures [S2].
- FAA AC 43-206 defines intergranular corrosion chemically at grain boundaries but does not provide repair procedures for 2024/7075 in the supplied excerpts [S3].

Where to look:
- For the abrasive blasting prohibition: FAA AC 43-4B: Corrosion Control for Aircraft, location 106 [S4].
- For the description of exfoliation: FAA AC 43-4B: Corrosion Control for Aircraft, location 18 (Section 2.5.6) [S1].
- For additional context on intergranular corrosion definition (not repair): FAA AC 43-206 CHG1, location 26 [S3].
- For material susceptibility notes (not aircraft repair guidance): NASA-STD-6016C, location 92 [S2].

Warnings from the source documents on this topic:
- "Do not use abrasive blasting to remove intergranular corrosion." [S4]

query: How do stainless steel helicoil or wire inserts influence galvanic corrosion in aluminum assemblies?
answer:
Direct answer:
The supplied excerpts do not describe how stainless steel helicoil or wire inserts influence galvanic corrosion in aluminum assemblies; they only note that plated stainless inserts caused more corrosion of the aluminum than bare stainless inserts and that steel inserts caused more corrosion than cadmium-coated ones [S3]. They also state that stainless steels generally do not exhibit red rust and should be assessed with specific criteria [S1], and that the most practical means of controlling corrosion on non-plated steel is complete removal of corrosion products by mechanical means and maintaining a protective coating system, usually plating [S1]. No excerpt provides a method or sequence for inserting helicoils/wire inserts, nor does it detail the galvanic mechanism specific to those fasteners.

Where to look:
- For general corrosion control guidance on steel and stainless steel (including plating requirements): FAA AC 43-4B, location 30 [S1].

- For comparative corrosion results between plated vs bare stainless inserts and cadmium coatings (relevant to galvanic behavior but not specific to helicoils/wire inserts): NASA report on galvanic corrosion with aluminum/stainless inserts, location 7 [S3].

Warnings from the source documents on this topic:
None of the supplied excerpts contains a caution specifically about inserting or removing stainless steel helicoil or wire inserts that matches the question topic; the only caution present concerns switching off electrical power before inserting/removing items to avoid transient voltages causing permanent damage, which is unrelated to galvanic corrosion [S6].
